ful-medames.name: Ful medames
ful-medames.summary: A stew of cooked fava beans seasoned with olive oil and spices, considered Egypt's national dish and a staple food there since at least the 17th century.

mulukhiyah.name: Mulukhiyah
mulukhiyah.summary: A traditional Egyptian and Arab dish made from the leaves of a jute plant, cooked into a thick, mucilaginous broth or stew and usually served with rice.

kashk.name: Kashk
kashk.summary: A dried dairy product made from strained yogurt or buttermilk, popular across Iranian, Caucasian and Central Asian cuisines, known variously as kashk, qurut or keshk.

fesikh.name: Fesikh
fesikh.summary: A traditional Egyptian dish of salted, fermented mullet eaten mainly during the spring Sham Ennessim festival, with roots traced back to accounts by Herodotus.

saint-mark-s-coptic-orthodox-cathedral-a.name: Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral, Azbakeya
saint-mark-s-coptic-orthodox-cathedral-a.summary: Coptic Orthodox church in Azbakeya, Cairo, built after long Ottoman restrictions on church construction were eased, and the seat of the Coptic Pope from 1800 to 1971.
saint-mark-s-coptic-orthodox-cathedral-a.source_title: Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral, Azbakeya

azbakeya.name: Azbakeya
azbakeya.summary: A district formed by Cairo's 19th-century expansion beyond its medieval walls, home to the historic Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral.

yuhanna-al-armani.name: Yuhanna al-Armani
yuhanna-al-armani.summary: Armenian artist in Ottoman Egypt (1726–1786) best known for religious works, especially Coptic icons decorating The Hanging Church in Old Cairo.

french-invasion-of-egypt-and-syria.name: French invasion of Egypt and Syria
french-invasion-of-egypt-and-syria.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte's 1798–1801 military expedition to Ottoman-held Egypt and Syria, aimed at weakening British trade and power, ending in French withdrawal.
french-invasion-of-egypt-and-syria.source_title: French invasion of Egypt and Syria

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

eyalet.name: Eyalet
eyalet.summary: A major administrative province of the Ottoman Empire from 1453 until the early 19th century, governed by a beylerbey with broad military, financial and judicial powers.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

pasha.name: Pasha
pasha.summary: A high-rank Ottoman title granted by the Sultan to governors, generals and dignitaries, roughly equivalent to a British Lord; also used in Egypt and Morocco.

upper-egypt.name: Upper Egypt
upper-egypt.summary: The southern portion of Egypt, running along the Nile valley south of the delta from Beni Suef down to Lake Nasser.

rosetta.name: Rosetta
rosetta.summary: A Nile Delta port city in Egypt, near where the Rosetta Stone was found in 1799; founded around the 9th century, it later became a popular 19th-century British tourist stop.

athanasius-kircher.name: Athanasius Kircher
athanasius-kircher.summary: German Jesuit scholar (1601/1602 to 1680) who published around 40 works and correctly linked ancient Egyptian to Coptic, sometimes regarded as a founder of Egyptology.

coptic-language.name: Coptic language
coptic-language.summary: The last stage of the Egyptian language, spoken from the 3rd century AD and written in the Coptic alphabet; replaced by Arabic but still used in church liturgy.

oedipus-aegyptiacus.name: Oedipus Aegyptiacus
oedipus-aegyptiacus.summary: Athanasius Kircher's 17th-century work of Egyptology attempting to translate Egyptian hieroglyphs from the Bembine Tablet, later shown by scholars to be inaccurate.

georges-cuvier.name: Georges Cuvier
georges-cuvier.summary: French naturalist and zoologist (1769-1832) considered the founding father of paleontology, who established comparative anatomy and proved that species could go extinct.

craniometry.name: Craniometry
craniometry.summary: The measurement of the human skull, once used in the 19th and early 20th centuries to support pseudoscientific theories of racial hierarchy, though still used today by forensic and physical anthropologists.

anthropometry.name: Anthropometry
anthropometry.summary: The systematic measurement of the human body's size and shape, used historically in physical anthropology and today in fields like industrial design and ergonomics.

constantin-fran-ois-chasseb-uf-comte-de-.name: Volney
constantin-fran-ois-chasseb-uf-comte-de-.summary: French philosopher, historian, and orientalist (1757–1820), known by his pen name Volney, who traveled through Ottoman Egypt and Syria and later served in French revolutionary government.
constantin-fran-ois-chasseb-uf-comte-de-.source_title: Constantin François Chassebœuf, comte de Volney

vivant-denon.name: Vivant Denon
vivant-denon.summary: French artist, writer, diplomat and archaeologist (1747–1825) who became the first director of the Louvre after Napoleon's Egyptian campaign; his 1802 travel account helped found modern Egyptology.

funj-sultanate.name: Funj Sultanate
funj-sultanate.summary: An Islamic kingdom in what is now Sudan, founded in 1504 by Sultan Amara Dunqas at its capital Sennar, reaching its peak in the late 17th century before an 1821 Turco-Egyptian conquest ended it.

makuria.name: Makuria
makuria.summary: Medieval Nubian kingdom, capital Dongola, in what is now northern Sudan and southern Egypt; it repelled an Arab invasion in 652 and kept a resulting peace treaty for six centuries.

alodia.name: Alodia
alodia.summary: Medieval Christian kingdom in what is now central Sudan, with its capital at Soba, that thrived as a multicultural trading hub roughly from the 6th century until around 1500.

amara-dunqas.name: Amara Dunqas
amara-dunqas.summary: First ruler of the Kingdom of Sennar, reigning from 1504 to about 1533/4, who founded the city of Sennar and used diplomacy to keep Ottoman forces from conquering his realm after 1517.

sennar.name: Sennar
sennar.summary: A city on the Blue Nile in Sudan that served for centuries as capital of the Funj Kingdom of Sennar and later of Sennar State.

al-ashraf-qansuh-al-ghuri.name: Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghuri
al-ashraf-qansuh-al-ghuri.summary: Penultimate Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, reigning from 1501 to 1516, one of the last and most powerful rulers of the Burji dynasty.

selim-i.name: Selim I
selim-i.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520, known as Selim the Grim, whose conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Levant made the Ottoman Empire the leading Muslim power.

shaykh-al-balad.name: Shaykh al-Balad
shaykh-al-balad.summary: A political and administrative title in Ottoman Egypt that, by the 18th century, was held by leading Mamluks whose authority often rivaled the Ottoman governor's.

amir-al-hajj.name: Amir al-Hajj
amir-al-hajj.summary: A title given to the commander of the annual Hajj pilgrim caravan under successive Muslim empires from the 7th to 20th centuries, responsible for funding, provisioning and protecting pilgrims to Mecca and Medina.

qaitbay.name: Qaitbay
qaitbay.summary: Mamluk Sultan of Egypt from 1468 to 1496 who stabilized the state's economy, fought the Ottomans, and was a major patron of architecture across the region.

tuman-bay-ii.name: Tuman Bay II
tuman-bay-ii.summary: The last Mamluk Sultan of Egypt, ruling briefly before the Ottoman conquest of 1517; a former palace slave who rose to become prime minister.

dawatdar.name: Dawadar
dawatdar.summary: A senior court office, meaning 'keeper of the inkpot', created under the Seljuks and later one of the most powerful positions in the Mamluk Sultanate.

badi-iv.name: Badi IV
badi-iv.summary: Ruler of the Kingdom of Sennar from 1724 to 1762, also called Badi abu Shilluk, whose forces defeated an invading Ethiopian army in 1738 before he was deposed by his own son and later killed in captivity.

hamaj-regency.name: Hamaj Regency
hamaj-regency.summary: A political order in central Sudan (1762-1821) in which the Funj sultans of Sennar kept the throne while Hamaj regents held the real power.

al-mutawakkil-iii.name: al-Mutawakkil III
al-mutawakkil-iii.summary: The seventeenth Abbasid caliph of Cairo under Mamluk authority, holding the position from 1508 to 1516 and again in 1517.

al-azhar-university.name: Al-Azhar University
al-azhar-university.summary: Founded in Cairo in 970 by the Fatimid Caliphate, it is Egypt's oldest university and one of the most prestigious centers of Islamic learning in the world.

al-sha-rani.name: Al-Sha'rani
al-sha-rani.summary: Egyptian scholar (1492/3–1565) who was a jurist, historian, mystic and theologian, regarded as "one of the last original thinkers in Islam." He founded an Egyptian Sufi order that remained active until the 19th century.

murtada-al-zabidi.name: Murtada al-Zabidi
murtada-al-zabidi.summary: Indian-born Sunni scholar (1732-1790) based in Cairo, regarded as the greatest hadith scholar of his time. He was also a leading philologist, lexicographer, historian and mystic.

madhhab.name: Madhhab
madhhab.summary: School of thought within Islamic jurisprudence. The four major Sunni schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) emerged in the ninth and tenth centuries CE.

shadhili.name: Shadhili
shadhili.summary: A Sufi order founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili in the 13th century, historically influential in the Maghreb and Egypt and followed by millions worldwide.

arabization.name: Arabization
arabization.summary: Process of cultural change in which a non-Arab society adopts or is pushed toward Arabic language, culture and identity. It followed the Muslim conquests and later Arab nationalist policies.

ulama.name: Ulama
ulama.summary: Scholars and judges of Islamic doctrine and law, considered guardians, interpreters, and transmitters of religious knowledge, traditionally trained in madrasas.

sultanate-of-darfur.name: Sultanate of Darfur
sultanate-of-darfur.summary: Pre-colonial state in present-day Sudan lasting from the 16th century to 1874, stretching at its peak from Darfur to the White Nile.

badawiyya.name: Badawiyya
badawiyya.summary: Sufi order founded in 13th-century Egypt by Ahmad al-Badawi. It was hugely popular under the Mamluks and Ottomans and spread to Turkey, and its mawlid at Tanta is still celebrated yearly.

ahmad-al-badawi.name: Ahmad al-Badawi
ahmad-al-badawi.summary: 13th-century Sufi mystic born in Fes, Morocco, who founded the Badawiyyah Sufi order. He settled in Tanta, Egypt, in 1236 and died in 1276; his tomb remains a major site of devotional visits.

danagla.name: Danagla
danagla.summary: A Nubian tribe of northern Sudan settled near the Nile's third cataract, traditionally speaking a Nubian language now being replaced by Arabic.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

lower-nubia.name: Lower Nubia
lower-nubia.summary: Northernmost part of ancient Nubia, now largely submerged under Lake Nasser after the Aswan High Dam's construction, with its monuments relocated in a major 20th-century rescue effort.

al-maris.name: al-Maris
al-maris.summary: A medieval Arabic name for Lower Nubia, the Nile region around the first and second cataracts including Aswan, ruled at times by Fatimid Egypt, the Ayyubids, and Christian kings at Dotawo until 1504.

tariqa.name: Tariqa
tariqa.summary: A religious order within Sufism, the mystical tradition of Islam, led by a spiritual guide and followed by members seeking a closer personal relationship with God.

dhikr.name: Dhikr
dhikr.summary: An Islamic devotional practice of repeatedly reciting prayers or God's names to remember God, central to Sufism and often performed with set postures, breathing, or movement.

david-ben-solomon-ibn-abi-zimra.name: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra
david-ben-solomon-ibn-abi-zimra.summary: Rabbi and legal scholar (1479–1573), known as the Radbaz, who wrote more than 3,000 halakhic rulings and other scholarly works.
david-ben-solomon-ibn-abi-zimra.source_title: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra
